title: the things your family kept
hook: a medal on a keychain, a palm behind the crucifix, an abuela's altarcito: the Church's one word for all of it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lent, less on purpose. Six words so far: the sign of the cross, the Eucharist, confession, the rosary, the saints, Lent. Today, the seventh.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS · THE EUCHARIST · CONFESSION · THE ROSARY · THE SAINTS · LENT`

segments.voice: A Saint Christopher medal on a keychain. A palm from Palm Sunday tucked behind the crucifix, drying out for a year. A bottle of holy water in the kitchen cabinet. An abuela's altarcito, with candles, a rosary and photos of the people she's lost. A Santo Niño, the child Jesus, watching over a Filipino living room. A medal blessed at a quinceañera Mass. Every family's version looks different. The Church has one word for all of it.
screen: `A MEDAL. A PALM. HOLY WATER.` → `AN ALTARCITO. A SANTO NIÑO.` → `ONE WORD FOR ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Sacramentals. The word is a cousin of sacrament. The seven sacraments, like baptism, confession and the Eucharist, are the big moments Catholics believe Christ himself gave the Church. Sacramentals are the smaller things the Church added around them: blessings, blessed objects, words and gestures. Look back at this week and you'll find you've been holding them all along. Holy water and the sign of the cross. The ashes. The rosary. A saint's medal. The Church is careful about what they are. They aren't magic, and they aren't lucky charms. They're reminders that help a person get ready for grace, the way a photo on the fridge reminds you to call. Around them grows what the Church calls popular piety: the customs each people builds, which it welcomes as long as they lead back to Christ. So a Filipino family getting up before dawn for nine Masses before Christmas, called Simbang Gabi. A Mexican family's altar for its dead in early November. An Irish grandmother who won't eat meat on any Friday of the year. An Italian town's feast for its patron saint. Different shapes, one faith. Whatever your family's version was, it was a way in.
screen: `SACRAMENTS: THE BIG SEVEN.` · `SACRAMENTALS: THE SMALL SIGNS.` · `NOT MAGIC: REMINDERS.` · `DIFFERENT SHAPES, ONE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring to mind one object from your family's faith: a medal, a picture, a candle, a rosary in a drawer. On the first breath, see it. On the second, see whose it was. On the third, let it remind you of them.
Sacramentals. Small blessed things and gestures: reminders that point to grace. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: faith you can hold. That's week one: seven words, and you were already holding most of them. Tomorrow, your grandmother before dinner.

howItsDone: Catholics use sacramentals such as holy water, blessed medals, rosaries, palms and ashes, ask a priest to bless homes and objects, and keep the devotions of their own families and cultures, from home altars to Simbang Gabi and patron-saint feasts.

story.title: roses in December
story.text: On a cold December morning in 1531, an Indigenous man named Juan Diego is hurrying past a hill outside what is now Mexico City. A lady stops him there and asks him to tell the bishop to build her a church. The bishop wants proof. So she sends Juan Diego up the bare hilltop, where he finds roses blooming out of season, and he carries them down in his cloak. When he opens it in front of the bishop, the roses spill out, and on the cloth is her image. Mexican Catholics call her Our Lady of Guadalupe, and her picture stands on many family altars.
story.source: the traditional account of Our Lady of Guadalupe (the Nican Mopohua, a Nahuatl telling from the 1500s)

wrong.myth: medals, holy water and palms are lucky charms.

notes: NEW lesson (2026-10-06), from the research's proposed day 7 ('your people's version: quinceañeras, Simbang Gabi, saints' medals and family altars'), which closes week one by handing the lesson back to the learner's family. Word 'sacramentals' chosen because it names, in the Church's own term, things already met this week (holy water and the sign of the cross, ashes, the rosary) and the family objects in the hook.

Seven sacraments 'given by Christ' (CCC 1114) vs sacramentals 'instituted by the Church' (CCC 1667); sacramentals 'prepare us to receive grace' (CCC 1670), paraphrased as 'help a person get ready for grace'. Confirm.
'They aren't magic' rests on CCC 1670 and 2111 (superstition). Confirm wording.
Popular piety welcomed 'as long as they lead back to Christ' paraphrases CCC 1674–1676 and the 2001 Directory (discernment, purification, orientation to the liturgy). Confirm the plain summary.

Family examples are given as single families ('a Filipino family', 'a Mexican family', 'an Irish grandmother', 'an Italian town'), not as what every member of a culture does. Simbang Gabi: nine dawn (or anticipated evening) Masses, December 16–24. Mexican home altars for the dead in early November (Día de Muertos, around All Saints and All Souls); the voice does not name the festival, to avoid oversimplifying it. Confirm.
Quinceañera: a blessed medal is a common gift at the Mass of thanksgiving (Catholic Company); confirm phrasing 'a medal blessed at a quinceañera Mass'.

Story: Our Lady of Guadalupe told as the traditional account (December 1531; Juan Diego; roses; the tilma). The Church canonized Juan Diego in 2002; the historicity of the Nican Mopohua is debated by historians. The story says 'Mexican Catholics call her'; confirm framing and that 'many family altars' is acceptable.
Day 7 has no 'think' item (the check-in plays instead), as on the Hindu path.
